One of the finest guitar players and
music arrangers in this country, John
Farrar, has returned
to Melbourne
after a quick trip to America. Farrar
attended several recording sessions,
including one under producer Bones
Howe. He was also present at a re-
cording session which featured a group
called Timber, which is managed by
former Aussie thrush Lynne Randel's
husband. Farrar also met up with
former Melbourne radio man Ken
Sparkes.
William J. Walsh has been appoint-
ed managing director and chairman
of RCA Ltd. based in Sydney. Origi-
nally from the States, Walsh also re-
tains his position as regional manager
for Australasia. He has been general
manager of RCA's
record
division
in Australia since 1965. The former
managing
director
and
chairman,
John W. Tyler is returning to tfie U.S.
The world famed Vienna Boys Choir
back down under for an extensive na-
tion-wide tour. On this current tour,
their sixth since World War II, they'll
give a total of thirty five concerts.
Tamla-Motown's
Stevie
Wonder
knockin' em dead with his personal
stint
at the hotel Chevron's Silver
Spade Room in Sydney. Stevie will be
followed by such stars as Brenda Lee,
Earl Grant, Ella Fitzgerald, and Al
Martino. Later in the year Bill Medley
will also appear. Plans are also under-
way again to ensure that many top
names from overseas not only appear
in Sydney, but also make the trip
five hundred miles southward to Mel-
bourne, a city of comparable size.
Melbourne's Lido nightclub and Life
International are mentioned as pos-
sible venues. When its considered that
Melbourne record buyers are as avid,
if not more so than their Sydney
counter -parts; its ridiculous that an
arrangement of the sort now planned
doesn't exist. Currently the only Mel-
bourne
outlet
for
regular
appear-
ances of entertainers of a top calibre
is the Chevron Hotel. Britain's Helen
Shapiro recently ended a stint there,
and now MCA's Leapy Lee is appear-
ing.The record dispute:
The embargo
on the performance via radio of re-
cords originating out of Europe and
Australia continues. Only American
records are being aired together with
a handful of local discs produced on
independent labels which, unlike the
major disc concerns, are not demand-
ing any royalty
for
air -play.
This
handful of independents are becoming
stronger day by day, and as a para-
dox, many of them are either pressed
or linked in some way with the big
companies who are responsible for the
ban coming into being.
For instance, the most successful
"new" label born out of the present
dispute is Fable Records who have
Make sure that you are repre-
sented in the Annual Directory
Issue! Contact:
AUSTRALIA
PETER SMITH
40 Winters Way
Doncaster 3108
Victoria, Australia
no less than six singles riding the
charts. Fable is pressed by the Phil-
ips company who release on the Pho-
nogram label. Astor Records are dis-
tributing the Sweet Peach label which
is also okay for air -play here. Any day
now news is expected concerning RCA
who look like entering the field with
a new label featuring talent available
for air -play. The giant Festival Re-
cords company also has plans well
advanced for the same reason.
Meanwhile top
artists
here
con-
tracted to major labels are not being
heard on any of the 114 stations con-
trolled by the Commercial Federation
of Broadcasting Stations. Several of
the really big names on the disc scene
here told Cash Box
hat since the
dipute arose some months back they
have not had the courtesy of being
informed of their position by their
respective
labels.
Understandably
they're hopping mad about the lack of
air -play, as this results in a slacken-
ing -off with regards to personal ap-
pearances. (The main income for a
personality here is derived, not from
the actual record, but from the de-
mand
it
creates
for
appearances
around the country.) The same artists
informed Cash Box
hat if the situa-
tion does not change in the immediate
future, they will be organising a na-
tional conference of all recording art-
ists affected by the dispute. In the
meantime, enterprising television sta-
tions who have in recent times turned
a blind eye to demands for pop music
shows, have now brought into being
several new teen -styled programmes
aimed at supplying the demand which
radio stations are not meeting be-
cause of the ban. The two most power-
ful networks have music shows al-
ready under way with two of
this
country's
hottest properties Ronnie
Burns and John Farnham.
Various
predictions
have
been
made as to when the dispute will end,
but as we go to press there is de-
finitely no end in sight. The major
record companies meanwhile are mis-
sing out on an increasing amount of
revenue because all their records of
local or British/European origin are
not being played.
Nevertheless
all
reports seem to indicate that the big
companies producers are still hard at
work inside the studios creating many
new sides, just as if nothing had hap-
pened. This is perhaps the only real
indication that maybe the end of the
dispute is in sight. That however is
mere guess -work. Only a handful of
executives at
the top know whats
going
on, and they're
not
talking!

Velvet Underground
Back On N.Y. Scene
NEW YORK —
The
Velvet
Under-
ground
will make
its
first New York
appearance in three years. Upstairs at
Max’s
Kansas
City
Restaurant,
on
June
24. The date commences
a two
show per night engagement which will
run—except for the nights
of June 29
and 30 through July 5.
Their return to New York marks the
end of the Velvet’s self-imposed exile
from
a scene which they themselves
had done much
to
invent.
Their
last
performance here was at the now de-
funct Gymnasium in April 1967. In the
two years prior to that date, the Vel-
vet
Underground
had
played
exten-
sively
in
this
area. The
highlight
of
this
period was
the
group’s
engage-
ment at the Ballroom Farm (now The
Electric Circus)
on St. Marks’
Place,
with Andy Warhol’s Exploding Plastic
Inevitible, a mixed media show.
In
recent
years,
the Velvet Under-
ground
has
been
playing
regularly
outside of New York. After recording
three albums for MGM, the group this
year signed a recording contract with
Atlantic.
Their
first
Atlantic
album,
produced by Adrian Barber,
is due for
July release.

Dowden & Co. Custom
-Anniversary’ Albums
PHILADELPHIA — Two custom
“Col-
lector’s Edition” record albums, creat-
ed exclusively for U.
S. corporations
and groups celebrating 25th or 50th an-
niversaries in 1970 and 1971, are being
produced by Dowden & Company, Phil-
adelphia anniversary consulting firm.
The 50th anniversary album, entitled
“Golden Hits for a Golden Anniversa-
ry”, includes 19 classic old and new all-
time best
sellers, spanning the years
from 1920 to 1970. Included:
“Charles-
ton,”
(1920), “Night and Day”
(1932).
“Oklahoma!”
(1943), “76 Trombones”
(1957),
“Hello,
Dolly”
(1964),
“Hey,
Jude”
(1968),
and
“Raindrops Keep
Failin’ on My Head”
(1970). Artists in-
clude Benny Goodman, Harry James,
Aretha
Franklin,
Kostelanetz, Robert
Goulet, Ray Cmckf, Peter Nero, etc.
The 25th anniversary album features
the Academy Award Winners song for
each of the past 25 years, by top
re-
cording stars.
Both records are designed for use by
the golden and
silver corporate
cele-
brants
as executive
gifts,
premiums,
traffic
builders,
self-liquidators
and
incentives.
The entire
right inner panel
of the
gate-fold record jacket is reserved for
any custom use a celebrant
dictates:
a letter from the president, a concise
corporate history, etc. The other inner
jacket panel traces the evolution of the
music
- and the nation’s history over
the 25 and 50 year time periods respec-
tively.

Sam Goody Ups
Sales Earnings
MASPETH, NEW YORK —
Sam
Goody,
Inc. has the
results
of opera-
tions for the
first quarter and twelve
months ended March
31,
1970:
Earn-
ings
for
the
initial
1970
period
amounted to $57,900, or $.08 per share,
calculated on 683,000 shares,
as com-
pared with
$55,084,
or
$.08 per share
on 650,000 shares,
for the comparable
interval in 1969. Sales of the company
for the 1970 first quarter amounted to
an
initial period high of $5,024,556,
as
compared with
$3,584,507
reported
in
the same 1969 period.
For
the
trailing
twelve
months
ended March 31,
1970, sales amounted
to
$17,670,832,
as
compared
with
$14,579,813 recorded in the comparable
twelve months through March 31,
1969.
Earnings rose to $623,072, or
$.94 per
share,
as compared with
$383,703,
or
$.67
per
share
for
the
respective
twelve
months
periods.
The
twelve
months ended March 31,
1970 included
extraordinary
credits
of
$.11
per
share,
while
the
preceding
twelve
months
included
a
$.03
per
share
extraordinary charge.
Per share results for the 1969 periods
have
been
adjusted
for
the
2-for-l
stock split in December, 1969.
Sam
Goody,
president,
noted
that
start-up
costs
in
connection
with
establishment
of
the
new
wholesale
division, as well as
interest expenses
incurred
in
financing
the
acquisition,
prevented first quarter earnings from
expanding further.
Goody indicated that the company’s
ninth
retail
store
is
scheduled
for
opening
in Sept.
1970,
in the regional
King’s
Plaza
Shopping
Center
in
Brooklyn,
New
York,
and
that
the
company’s
tenth
unit
would
be
lo-
cated in a large shopping center being
constructed
in Woodbridge, New
Jer-
sey, which is scheduled for completion
in October, 1970.
Sam
Goody,
Inc.,
traded
over-the-
counter, presently operates a chain of
eight
retail audio and
record
stores.
Through
a
wholly-owned
subsidiary,
Brun-International Recotape Corpora-
tion,
the company
is also engaged
in
the wholesale distribution
of
records,
tapes and accessories.

Two-Way Information
On
the
initial
relase,
Alexenburg
will supply information
about
the
di-
rection
in which a
single
is expected
to be pushed. Decisions
for the direc-
tive are arrived at by discussions with
home office and field personnel. Based
on reactions, he will then send regular
directives
about
stations
to
contact
and areas or outlets that have begun
to move the single into other formats.
This gives MOR
singles the power
to
go
top
forty, R&B
records
a
shot
at
teen
sales
and
country
product
a
chance
to
sell
adult
or
top
forty.
“While it’s comforting to have success
with major acts, a tremendous amount
of satisfaction is
still in bringing about
something
with
new
artists.
A
first
hit for a new act is excellent, but get-
ting
a
million-seller
for
performers
who
are
not
teen
attractions
is
the
greatest feeling.”
Supplementing the
directives,
Alex-
exburg
is supplied with copies of cor-
respondence
between
national,
re-
gional and branch
representatives
to
stay on top of the situation developing
for a record.
Each week
is wrapped up by
run-
ning down the radio status of the prod-
uct and compiling
a
“master
sheet”
of
all stations playing product, where
the song is charted and how frequently
he
record
is played.
Separate
tallies
are compiled for top
forty, R&B and
country stations and these are on the
desks
of
all
field
people Monday
morning.
On
the
other
side,
Alexenburg
is
kept supplied with computer rundowns
of
sales
figures
with
totals
and
re-
gional breakdowns
to
reflect
growth
by area for various periods up to the
present.
These
include
LP’s
from
which
singles
can
be
pulled
using
added
information
from
radio
play-
list samplings.
“This gives us the power
to
follow
through
with
sales
by
assuring
that
stock
is supplied
to
cities where
the
material
is
played.”
It
also
allows
Alexenburg and his associates to keep
the trades and tip sheets aware of the
course
of
a
single
or album
on
the
sales
level. Handling disbursement of
this data are Steve Popovich, assistant
director
of
national
promotion;
Jim
Brown,
manager
of
album
promo;
Sheila
Chlanda,
supervisor
of promo
administration;
and
Nashville

TOP HITS OF THE YEAR
A COMPILATION OF THE YEAR'S BIGGEST HITS TO DATE
Because Cash Box is continually asked to supply a
list of the year’s leading hits to A&R men, record producers
and radio stations, etc.. Cash Box offers a continuing feature that lists the year's Top 50 titles as of the date the
feature appears. The feature is published in the last issue of each month and
is compiled from the Cash Box Top
100 Sales Chart Point system operates as follows: For each week a song
is #1 on the Top 100
it receives 135
points. Each #2-record is awarded 124 points. No. 3 gets 123. No. 4 gets 122. No. 5 gets 121. From No. 6 thru
No. 10 songs get 115 to 111 points respectively. No. 11 song gets 90 points and so on down the line
till the No. 50
song which gets 51 points. Only the top fifty titles of any given week are included
in the survey. Survey begins
with the first issue in January.

NEW YORK (Cont'd. from page 38
)
In the
fall, the company plans to start an intermediate priced concert program
which works on the same idea as the coffeehouse but
in
a concert format. The
deal would be for one or two nights packaging one or two performers
for each
concert. Act might get from $200 to $1,500 for a concert.
Again,
it’s something
that the schools could afford, concerts that big agencies wouldn’t bother to handle
because of the money involved and
it also gives the performer someplace to go
after the coffeehouse circuit.
The Bitter End network
is the only circuit of this nature
in the country. Thirteen
circuit coordinators handle the colleges
in the various areas throughout the coun-
try.
All the colleges are kept informed
of what’s happening by
a monthly news-
letter.
One of the other things
in the works
is a film circuit
in which specialized films
like an Incredible String Band concert film, or a film on woman’s liberation could
be passed around the circuit. A part of the plans call for a Movie Or^ which em-
ploys a concept of piecing together
bits of film and sound
for a
six hour show
that has no plot but a central theme, so that anyone could enter or leave during
its runningtimeand not miss anything.
The main thing about Campus
Directions
is that out of one office comes the
management, booking and
publishing facilities necessary for an
act. The whole
idea of the company
is sound and
is one of the most promising things to actually
be working within the American folk and rock scene. Such artists as John Denver,
Jerry
Jeff Walker, McKendrie
Spring,
Keith
Sykes, Townes Van Zandt and
Don
Crawford have been a part of the coffeehouse circuit and have gotten the proper
exposure each of them needed from
it. As a certain
publicity director said about
Mike Brovsky and his whole idea: “His head
is
in the right place.” Maybe instead
of going
after the
big,
big money and
the
big,
big
bands, some
other heads
throughout the country could start turning in the right direction.
fred holman
EAST COAST GIRL OF THE WEEK
Would you
call a Swedish
girl who married an
Italian a Swedish Meatball? Not
if she was Karin Grasso of Tonsil
Records, where she
is a production
assistant,
sales person, bookkeeper, song publishing aide,
etc. Married
to BMI
songwriter
Richard Grasso of Beechwood Music, Karin
is 25 years old. She says, though, that
she’s been in the record/entertainment business for a hundred years!
As a teenager she worked
in
her home
town Miami with three dj’s as Radio
Girl,
giving
nightly
reports
on
the
Top
10
songs and the local scene. Upon gradua-
tion (two days after to be exact) she was
on a plane to New York where she turned
up
a
job
as
a
dancer—something
she
had done
in Miami. She was a
"twister”
at the Peppermint Lounge, The
Round-
table,
Trudy
Heller’s
and
other
clubs
around
town.
She
also worked
at
free
lance fashion modeling during what she
calls her “ultra-skinny days” and appears
on a few Blue Note album covers. For 3
years she worked as
Roulette
president
Morris Levy’s secy, and for 2Vz years she
held
a
job
at
Liberty.
The
opportunity
came up
late
last
year
to work
with
a
new
record company from
scratch
and
took it—Tonsil, started
in January, 1970,
and now has one LP and two singles. She
loves her work and, between her hobbies
of
cooking
and
athletics,
finds
a
few
hours a day for
it.
SHORTTAKES
When a group sits down to create a name that
it can go under, the members
must always have things to say about words and phrases that
will be associated
with
it — complimentary or derogatory.
Gulliver, a new group on
Elektra, must
have had fun thinking about record
reviews
that would say ”...
a group that
stands
tall” or “Watch for this one to travel way up the charts.” The possibilities
are endless depending on your familiarity with English
literature (Jonathan
Swift
in particular) or your talent for making puns. While you mull over a few ideas on
this matter,
let me
fill you
in on the group.
I mentioned their album several weeks
ago and
it is
still one of my favorites to come from an American (Philadelphian
in
particular) group
in a long time. They came up and rapped about how they
re-
corded
it to get such clarity on the recording. The quartet, composed of ex-music
students, an ex-art student and an ex-transient apple picker/drive-in theatre
at-
tendant, have
all worked among one of the three dies of Philadelphia studio men
over the past two years. Together they have cut with The Electric
Indian, Assem-
bled Multitude and others. So, studio techniques are very familiar to them and the
group uses them to their
fullest to enhance their songs. And they say that the
strongest thing working
for them
is each
of
their songs which
are simple and
flowing without a single unnecessary
frill added. Harmonies and choise of instru-
mentation are tactfully chosen and worked out. The group says they go
into the
studio knowing what to do and go
after
a
tight,
full and coherent sound. The
quietly amplified set-up
of the studio makes
it their creative workshop and
the
album they have produced
is a masterpiece.
It’ll be out soon and the group
will
be promoting
it on-stage.
(I’ll
not end
this item with
a
blasted pun about these
potential giants.)
Two of the most promising happenings slated
for the New York area this sum-
mer — Mountaindaie and the New York Pop Concerts — are beginning to turn less
turn
less promising each day.
It seems that Brave New World, the producers of
the NYPC,
is forcing several top acts slated for both tests on the July 11 and 17
weekends to be withdrawn from the Mountaindaie
bill because of a lOO-mile/21-
day exclusivity clause
in the contracts they signed with various agencies. Moun-
taindaie is trying to replace the acts with others, and seems to be doing a good job
of
it considering the odds. This is one to keep an eye on. Meanwhile the only peo-
ple who are really suffering from the rip-off are ticket holders who are anxious of

)
official
photographers
of Concert
Associates,
California’s
leading
promoters.

addition to album covers, concerts and P.R. pictures, Emerson-Loew are also work-

The pictures on the lower two-thirds of this page were
all shot at the Who con-

LOUIE, LOUIE “As
long as those
pearly teeth
hold
out,
Louie’ll
still
be
playing
something new, and
all the others
will be running after him, trying to catch up.”
(Jazz pianist Richard M. Jones)
If anyone should ask we’d say that Louie Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Benny
Goodman are the Bach, Beethoven and Brahms of jazz. And
if we had to name
one guy alone, we’d
give
Louis the
title as the greatest jazz
personality ever
to
raise a horn to his lips and blast a rooftop.
Armstrong
is 70 years old — today. He has been blowing
into a trumpet (and
cornet) for nearly 60 out of those 70 barrelhouse years. The history books
tell us
that he started
in New Orleans, fooling around with a beatup trumpet and trying
it on for size. He was twelve when he was sentenced to the Waif’s home for “firing
firearms within the city limits.” And it was there that he learned to read music.
By 1917 he was playing
in the excursion boats that moved up the Mississippi’s
muddy waters. By 1922 he was
a member of King Oliver’s band
at the Lincoln
Garden
in Chicago. And two years
later he was the
star attraction with
Fletcher
Henderson’s band at the Roseland in N.Y. By 1927 he had moved
into the Sunset
Cafe with his own band. But Louis was always — and
will always be — the main
attraction. So eloquent, so unique that kids who had jazz within them came nightly
to listen
in awe-struck devotion. Kids who were screwballs at the time — Muggsy
Spanier, Bing Crosby, Frank Teschmacher, Bix Beiderbecke, Jess Stacy and Benny
Goodman.
What Armstrong did those nights at the Sunset he
is
still doing. And
if he occa-
sionally hams
it up a
bit, we understand.
It was
in the mid-thirties when
Holly-
wood finally discovered him — handed him a scene or two in a Crosby flick (“Pen-
nies From Heaven”) and Louis became a kind of clown. And
in “Going Places” he
crooned Johnny Mercer’s “Jeepers Creepers” (where’d you get those peepers?”) to
a horse. Louis probably came off best in “Nnew Orleans,” a film based loosely on
his
life. To our recollection
it was (and probably
still
is) the most authentic jazz
incorporated into a film score.
Now he can be caught on TV occasionally, guesting on shows helmed
by far
lesser talents than him. And
in Europe, where he
is revered,
he’ll tour to standing
room only crowds with pick up
all star combos. Soon
he’ll be
in town, we hear, to
celebrate his 70th with us, concertizing and compelling.
This then (since we don’t have his home address)
is our open-adoration birthday
greeting to the King. Stick with the Swiss Kriss, man. Happy 70th.
A post-script on Ellington (also celebrating his 70th this year) who
is currently
represented with a two pocket Solid State (Transamerica)
LP, cut
in Manchester,
England
last November. We heard the LP just this morning. And we’re planning
to take
it to bed tonight. To our ears they’re the best Ellington sides since he
left
Victor ...and that’s a long longtime.
AND HOWE — Last week’s announcement that Macey Lipman and Bones Howe
had joined forces to form a new production firm (Mr. Bones Productions), we hear,
has been
in the works for months. As a matter of fact songsmith Norman Gimbel
mentioned
it to us when we were
in N.Y.
in April.
“It’s not definite,” said Norman.
“I called Macey the other day but he refused comment.” Another case of Macey
nottellingGimbel — no?
harveygeller

'Rock’s’ Roxon Tells
Biz Execs To Turn On
To Rock Generation
NEW YORK — Lillian Roxon,
author
of the “Rock Encyclopedia,” has warn-
ed business executives that the “busi-
ness community must tune in to youth
before youth tunes the business com-
munity out.”
Miss
Roxon
made
these
remarks
last week
(24) while serving as moder-
ator of a discussion on the “Impact of
Rock Music on Business,” held at Trin-
ity Church on Wall Street. She empha-
sized that the “youth of today not only
possess a major portion of the buying
power in our economy but are also the
trend setters. Wide
ties, tie-dyed fash-
ions,
1970
cars
and
most
up-to-date
fashions can be directly traced to our
youth and to their idols
.
.
. rock musi-
cians.”
Miss Roxon further suggested, “It is
time
that middle
class,
middle
aged
business executives, who for the most
part control business, give youth a big-
ger break.” She called for the creation
of a “Little Brother Program.” Young
people would “adopt”
a Businessman
and thus serve as a direct
line to the
pulse of the younger generation.
Appearing
on
the
panel
with
Miss
Roxon were:
Bruce Morrow, TV and
radio
personality;
Herb
Goldberg,
president of Contact Slacks Division of
Miller Bros. Hat Coim.;
George Kias,
Coca Cola
Bottling Company
of New
York; Miss R. Vivian Sargent, Person-
nel Officer at Chemical Bank; Alan M.
Augustine. Plymouth Motors; and Fa-
ther John Moody, Trinity Church.
Presenting a copy of the “Rock En-
cyclopedia” to Father Moody of Trini-
ty Church, Miss Roxon expressed the
hope that her book would serve as a
useful guide to business executives who
wish a bridge to the world of the young.

release.

pre-

to the coast
in mid-

the “Partridge Family,”

stars Shirley Jones and David Cassidy.

Hartman To Address COPME 
cashbox I 
stage 
Modern Jazz Quartet 
RAINBOW GRILL, NYC - The Mod- 
ern Jazz Quartet found itself in what 
even for this group was a slightly un- 
familiar setting when they opened an 
engagement last week at the Rainbow. 
But although the MJQ is not a tradi- 
tional supper club attraction, and de- 
spite the occasional misplacing of a 
fork or spoon during the set, the Quar- 
tet kept the audience intrigued via 
their musical expertise and the sheer 
dynamics of their instrumental inter- 
action. 
The MJQ opened with a few stan- 
dards, "Willow Weep For Me," "It 
Ain't Necessarily So," before doing a 
couple of more contemporary items, 
Tim Hardin's "Misty Roses" and Len- 
non-McCartney's "Yesterday." On the 
last named song, pianist John Lewis 
set down the melody, while vibist Milt 
Jackson overlaid a particularly imag- 
inative improvisational track. 
Turning to some original material, 
the group offered an excerpt from 
Lewis' score for the film, "Kemek," 
which was premiered in its entirety 
during last year's Christmas concert at 
Lincoln Center. Also from the Lewis 
catalog were "The Jasmine Tree," 
"Visitor From Mars," and the even 
more astral "Visitor From Venus." 
These offered Connie Kay the oppor- 
tunity to work with a variety of per- 
cussive instruments and the remark- 
able sounds he produced are probably 
still reverberating lightly somewhere 
in the room. 
The MJQ has been playing together 
for close to two decades now. But 
whereas many groups would have set- 
tled into a comfortable rut, this in- 
credible foursome has shunned the 
easy and obvious, opting instead for 
the adventurous. Both individually and 
collectively they have continued to 
strike out along new jazz routes and 
apparently they plan to continue walk- 
ing point. As well they should. 
e.k. 
The Kinks/Toe Fat 
WHISKY A GO-GO, L.A. - Head Kink 
Ray Davies generously told an enthu- 
siastic audience at a recent Whiskey A 
Go Go outing, "We're not a good group 
and we know it, but we enjoy ourselves 
His statement was half right. The 
Kinks do enjoy themselves and get 
further into it when the people out 
there get turned on to their music and 
performance, as they did at the Whis- 
key. The Kinks are a good group, ac- 
tually two different groups, in effect, 
with different approaches on records 
and in concert, putting out an incred- 
ible amount of energy in both capaci- 
ties. 
I've been a Kinks fan right from the 
beginning, when they unleashed "You 
Really Got Me" and "All Day and All 
of the Night" about five years ago, 
during the first wave of the British in- 
vasion. They epitomized raw rock and 
roll with those tunes and witi the fire 
and appeal of lead singer Davies and 
his cohorts in personal appearances. 
Strangely 
enough, 
they 
never 
achieved complete recognition, even as 
their music got more subtle and com- 
plex, from "Well Respected Gentle- 
man" and "Sunny Afternoon" to the 
recent "Arthur," scored for a televi- 
sion drama and a monumental contri- 
bution to recorded rock. 
The current Kinks include, besides 
Davies, John Dalton on bass, Dave 
Davies playing lead guitar and adding 
vocals, Mick Avory on drums and elec- 
tric piano -organist John Kirksey. On 
wax, most notably with "Arthur," the 
band exhibits an always -changing in- 
ventiveness over a solid, energetic rock 
base, whether using full brass or a sin- 
gle delicate harpischord line. 
On stage the Kinks harken back to 
their early days, still lively, explosive, 
appealing, even lovable, when, for in- 
stance, Ray Davies winks and points 
naughtily at the audience or when 
brother Dave shakes his shaggy locks 
and belts his raucous off-key vocals. 
(A note: Ray Davies has to be one 
of the most exciting singers in pop mu- 
sic. His wobbly, almost drunken deliv- 
ery and his beautifully timed move- 
ments put him up there beside the oft - 
lauded theatrics of Jagger, Morrison 
and Joplin.) 
At their Whiskey gig, the Kinks con- 
centrated on pure energy flow, using 
mostly old material and molding two 
guitars, bass, piano, drums and vocal 
harmonies into 
a 
pulsing electric 
machine. They did a haunting, strong 
"Waterloo Sunset; " "Brainwashed," 
from "Arthur," which equals Kinks in 
its unrelenting drive; the mystical 
"Big Sky," from the "Village Green 
Preservation 
Society" 
album 
and 
ended the set with a "Really Go Me - 
All Day" medley which almost blew 
them off the stage. 
They also fell into a fifties rock jam 
and kicked it all out with Chuck Berry - 
Little Richard licks. Dave Davies' 
playing, while not jaw -dropping, was 
consistently together. 
It might also be noted that drummer 
Avory holds his left hand stick in the 
time-honored manner, cradled in the 
crotch of his thumb and forefinger, 
rather than using it overhand like a 
club, an all too annoying mannerism of 
many rock drummers. And what could 
be heard of Kirksey's keyboard was 
pretty and powerful. 
As a publicity representative said 
later, most of the audience was made 
up of old Kinks fans. "You're either a 
Kinks freak or you're not," she said. 
She's probably right. 
I only caught part of Toe Fat's set. 
That new English group played before 
the Kinks minus their lead singer, who 
blew his voice in earlier sets. What 
was left was an electric blues instru- 
mental trio, adequate but all too famil- 
iar. 
s.s. 
Leon Thomas 
VILLAGE VANGUARD, NYC - When 
Leon Thomas arrives on the stage, you 
get the feeling something good is about 
to take place. Maybe it's the clothes he 
wears, which are beautiful and multi- 
hued. But you think, no, it's the man's 
exuberance, which is evident in his 
shuffling gait and his expression. Then 
he gets to shaking a cowbell, blowing 
a panpipe and throat articulating and 
you forget about the whys as you ex- 
perience the performance of an impor- 
tant new talent. 
During his five day stint at the Van- 
guard, Leon was working with 
a 
smaller group than the one heard on 
his recently released Flying Dutchman 
album. The compactness of the unit 
was well suited to the Vanguard. Off 
the LP came "One" and "Echoes," 
two songs written by the artist, fol- 
lowed by "The Creator Has A Master 
Plan (Peace)," co-authored by Phar- 
aoh Sanders. On this one Leon soon 
had the audience joining in; it spiraled 
upward to a joyful ending. The artist 
also offered an eloquent reading of 
Horace Silver's "Song For My Father." 
Leon deals in a sound which reaches 
into the consciousness of his listeners. 
Using his voice as an instrument and 
weaving his percussive patterns, the 
artist calls up spirits of his ancestors 
and creates an atmosphere which is 
as mental and spiritual as it is musical. 
Not exactly your run of the mill jazz- 
man, Leon Thomas. 
e.k. 
Bass Promoted To 
Chess Exec Producer 
CHICAGO - Ralph Bass has been pro- 
moted from producer at Chess Rec- 
ords to executive producer with the 
label. Bass will now supervise the en- 
tire Chess staff of producers for the 
Chicago -based record complex's Chess, 
Checker, Cadet and Cadet/Concept la- 
bels. 
A producer with Chess for 26 years, 
Bass brought Etta James, Moms Mab- 
ley, Pigmeat Markham and Mitty Col- 
lier to the label. 
Before joining Chess, Bass produced 
for Black and White, Savoy and King 
Records. He produced James Brown's 
"Please, Please, Please" for King as 
well as Earl Bostic's instrumentals for 
that label. Records by the Dominoes 
and the Royals on King were also pro- 
duced by Bass. ("Open The Door Rich- 
ard" by Jack McVey was his first hit 
production.) 
Other major R&B acts that Bass 
has produced are T -Bone Walker, 
Hank Ballard and the Midnighters, 
Johnny Otis and Winonie Harris. With 
Chess, Bass has worked in jazz as well 
as R&B, producing records by such 
artists as Ramsey Lewis.

Composer Tobias Dies 
NEW YORK - Charles Tobias, com-

died in New York at the age of 72. He 
was the writer of such songs as "Miss

NEW YORK (Con't. from Page 39) 
Everybody loves every kind of music - a comprehensive style of musical tastes." 
Then we spoke on his seminar work at colleges. He makes it clear that the text- 
book is one thing and his field work is another as far as jazz and all black music 
goes. Time was, even when he was in a black, Southern college himself, when jazz 
and other forms of black music were frowned upon by the faculty and he even 
cited that it was a matter for discipline if you were caught playing jazz in the re- 
hearsal halls. That's a lot of lost heritage which he says exists in some colleges 
even today. His whole band, all college graduates, take part in the two day semi- 
nar which includes several lectures on the roots and history of jazz and black 
music, concerts and workshops. It is usually set up in conjunction with a concert 
by the group at the college that week, sometimes being set up by the Black Stud- 
ies Program, a music or sociology or other department. In most cases the group 
does it free - Cannonball stated "There's no charge for the experience in black 
music." The concert generally pays it back. We talked about his thoughts on stu- 
dent unrest and things he observed during the heat of last semester. He claims 
he's non-violent and does not condone classroom burnings and the like because 
"It denies others of the right to study in that space." He talked about one incident 
at Berkeley where the rioters and administrators called a temporary truce in order 
to hold the annual two day jazz festival. For his seminar during the festival at- 
tended by 12,000 people, he drew 6000 of them in one day. This year his black 
music seminar program will be condensed into one four hour period. He's also 
trying to coordinate week-long workshops for credit, and a Southern black music 
festival which he would like to play with Clara Ward, Jerry Butler, Staple Singers, 
etc. Look for his new album and watch for him on campus and in concert hall - 
he knows what he's doing. 
EAST COAST GIRL OF THE WEEK 
For two years, Bonnie Belville has 
worked with Dave Glew and Sal Uterano 
of the Atlantic Album Sales Dept. Maybe 
you've heard her recently doing a Mott 
The Hoople, radio spot, or maybe you 
heard her a couple of years back at 
Palisades Park and other show spots 2nd 
soprano-ing with her singing group. 
She's also used that talent to land some 
session work. There's a whole story to 
the start and finish of that venture that 
is too long to get into now, but it does 
show off her go-getter spirit that served 
to land her jobs with CBS News and with 
several fashion shows as a model. On 
weekends she still uses the services of 
the Barbizon School of Modeling which 
she attended to get local fashion show 
work. Only recently did she begin taking 
guitar lessons but Bonnie claims, "Give 
me six months and 
I can truly boast of 
a little guitar."

Mountaindale was presented this week with an injunction by Sullivan County to 
foil plans for their summer activities, claiming a general lack of facilities to handle 
the crowds that are expected. So, the opening night Van Cliburn concert was can- 
celled until a later date, and the Mountaindale people are trying to iron things out 
in time for this weekend's rock fest. Set to appear is The Grateful Dead who will 
also be doing a set of concerts at The Fillmore this weekend, billed as "Dead At 
Midnight" - four nights of midnight concerts which will also feature a sub -group 
of Dead members performing under the title of The New Riders Of The Purple 
Sage. 
Mentioned the new McKendree Spring album last week. Well, this week 
I was 
able to hear one of the three acetates in existence of that group's Decca LP slated 
for August. All but two of the songs were penned by the group but one of the out- 
standing cuts is their interpretation of James Taylor's "Fire And Rain." Generally a 
fine album, it features a more fulfilling sample of their style than was found on 
their debut album. The group gave a tape of the new deck to the underground 
radio station at Cornell University. Requests for airplay was so strong after initial 
broadcasts, that one song went on the Top 30 charts there overnight, despite an- 
nouncements that the record was unavailable. The group appears at the Capitol 
Theatre very soon. 
Was also able to sneak a listen to the new Jerry Jeff Walker album on Atco. 
Recorded down South, there are some very strong production numbers that break 
up the "single" image of the singer -composer. Some say he will have a hard time 
trying to follow "Mr. Bojangles," but 
I think there is a lot in this album that could 
secure his career as a singer/songwriter. 
The Village Gate is onto a new rock format which will feature new groups 
throughout the week and weekends. Sunday nights will be set aside for experi- 
mentation in contemporary music forms, particularly jazz-rock fusion. That pro- 
gram kicks off on July 12 and 19 with groups Farmer Brown and The 7th Cen- 
tury. Call for reservations at GR 5-5120. 
A new horn section is working in the Muscle Shoals Studios in Alabama. Dale 
Quillen, Mike Stough, Stacy Goss and Sonny Royal play trombone, trumpet, fluegel- 
horn and tenor sax respectively, and double on F horn, bass trombone, tuba, 
Bari sax, alto sax and clarinet. The Shoals Horns have also been doing work at 
Tupelo, Mississippi's Triangle Sound Studios and at Quinvy Studios. 
This week's shows at the Schaefer Music Festival in the park are Ike & Tina 
Turner/Voices Of East Harlem on July 13, The Four Tops/Eddie Holman on the 
15th, Stan Kenton/Four Freshmen/Chris Connor on the 17th, and Little Richard/ 
Wayne Cochran & The C.C. Riders on Saturday (18). 
Les McCann and His Trio will play in the Garden of the Museum of Modern 
Art on the 16th. Muddy Waters is coming with his Blues Band on August 6th. 
There is a series of free concerts set for Tompkins Square Park on four con- 
secutive Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m. starting July 22 with two others on August 16 
in the afternoon and evening. Various concerts will feature gospel, folk, rock and 
jazz with a lot of local talent. Bring blankets and chairs. 
Poet/novelist/songwriter/singer Leonard Cohen will make his New York debut 
at the Forest Hills Music Festival on July 25. He'll be playing with his newly -formed 
band, The Army. He's now in Nashville recording his third Columbia album.

Can you identify our Mystery Man? Within the next two weeks a certain record 
industry individual will embark on a cross country bicycle trip. Though some have 
called his venture foolhardy, he has turned a deaf ear to their comments. He is 
undaunted. Having assembled the necessary items (tent, air mattress, maps, 
etc.) he stands tall, prepared to face the long and winding road to Los Angeles. 
Does the Easy Rider fate await him too? Or will he emerge as a modern day 
Lewis And Clark? And can you guess his identity? First correct answer received 
here at Cash Box will receive a special prize, donated by the Mystery Man him- 
self, a rare recording by Dolly Holiday. More clues next week.

Blue Thumb Readies 
2nd `Color Collage' LP 
LOS ANGELES - Having introduced 
its "Stereo Color Collage' multi -hued 
record with Dave Mason's album, 
"Alone Together," Blue Thumb Rec- 
ords next "Color Collage" LP will be 
"Buddy And The Juniors." This al- 
bum will be released in August. 
"Buddy And The Juniors" is the 
first time teaming of Buddy Guy, 
Junior Wells and Junior Mance. The 
project was conceived by Philadel- 
phia disk jockey Michael Cuscuna of 
WMMR-FM and financed by Blue 
Thumb. 
The colors used in this package 
differ significantly from those used 
on the Mason LP which is now Blue 
Thumb's top selling and fastest mov- 
ing album. Various grades of black 
and white are blended into the blues 
album, which features all accoustic 
instruments and no drums. 
The repertoire performed by ran- 
ges from "Talkin' Bout Women Ob- 
viously" to "Riffin," "Buddy's Blues," 
"Hoochie Coochie Man," "Five Long 
Years," "Rock Me Mama" and "Ain't 
No Need." 
Creedence Gold Album 
Heads Fantasy Release 
OAKLAND - "Cosmo's Factory," the 
new 
LP by Creedence Clearwater 
Revival-fifth in the series of LPs by 
Creedence-is a Gold Album as of 
the moment of release. Advance or- 
ders on the LP, which was released 
July 8, totaled over $1 million. 
The new Creedence LP contains 
seven original compositions by John 
Fogerty, lead singer and guitarist. 
Four of the songs in the LP have pre- 
viously been out on singles: "Up 
Around the Bend," "Run Through the 
Jungle," 
"Travelin' 
Band" 
and 
"Who'll Stop the Rain." Three of the 
songs are new. Fogerty produced the 
album. 
Included in the material on the LP 
is a Fogerty arrangement of "My 
Baby Left Me," a composition of vet- 
eran blues singer Arthur "Big Boys' 
Crudup, "Before You Accuse Me," 
one of Bo Diddley's hits, and "I 
Heard It Through The Grape Vine," 
standard. 
Also on the Fantasy July release 
schedule are two other new LPs, one 
by Billie Joe Becoat, "Let's Talk for 
Awhile" and "Parish Hall." 
Becoat's LP is his second for Fan- 
tasy (his first was released in 1969) . 
It was produced by Jesse Osborne. 
Parish Hall is a new group making its 
first recording debut with the Fantasy 
LP.

HELLO DARLIN' - Conway Twitty - Decca 
DL 75209 
Another country artist crosses the border into 
pop territory. Actually, Conway Twitty's done it 
before, but not in a while, and it was a surprise 
to find his single, "Hello, Darlin'," on the Top 
100. Now the album of the same name has hit 
the Top 100 Albums chart. Twitty is obviously 
an artist to be watched closely. His career may 
take some sudden turns. 
BLACK TALK! - Charles Earland - Prestige 
7758 
Jazz organist Charles Earland has come out 
of nowhere onto the charts. Assisted by Virgil 
Jones, trumpet; Houston Person, tenor sax; Mel- 
vin Sparks, guitar; Idris Muhammed, drums; 
and Buddy Caldwell, conga, Earland has made 
an album that has a wider appeal than any jazz 
organ set we can remember. LP has five selec- 
tions, including "Aquarius," "More Today Than 
Yesterday" (just released as a single) and the 
title tune. Watch this one closely for further ac- 
tion.

Pop Best Bets 
GREAT EXPECTATIONS - Kiki Dee - Tamla 
TS303 
Take one established British session singer, 
add an excellent record company that knows 
what it's about, sprinkle in arrangers and mu- 
sicians of style and taste building on rock solid 
songs and you have some idea of what this 
premier LP from Kiki Dee is like. But not quite. 
Here's a girl with one of the finest new voices 
around who has been struggling for some time 
in England with the wrong material. Suddenly, 
as happened when Dusty Springfield moved 
to Atlantic, Kiki's voice is finally liberated. Best 
cuts include "I Can't Give Back The Love and 
the moving "Jimmy."

THE CRUISIN' SERIES - Various Artists - In- 
crease INCM 2001-2007 
Increase Records, distributed by Chess, here 
offers "The Cruisin' Series," "A History Of Rock 
N'

sales in the cards for the series. 
Jazz Picks 
THE SIXTH SENSE - Lee Morgan --Blue Note 
BST 84335 
Lee Morgan, who as a teenager was already 
playing to acclaim in Dizzy Gillespie's band, 
has continued to seek out fresh musical direc- 
tions. The trumpet player adds another chapter 
to his story with an album which never lags 
in intensity of feeling and musical spirit. Though 
Morgan's presence is everywhere, the talents 
of his comrades in sound, four of whom are 
alumni of Art Blakey groups, contribute consid- 
erably to the LP's overall sound. Solid jazz entry. 
A DAY IN COPENHAGEN - Dexter Gordon - 
Prestige 7763 
Tenor sax man Dexter Gordon assembled a 
uniquely talented group of expatriate jazz musi- 
cians and they have come up with an album 
which is as refreshing as its title. Three Slide 
Hampton originals highlight a set which also in- 
cludes the contemporary standard, "The Shadow 
Of .Your Smile." Slide is heard on trombone and 
Kenny Drew offers some neat piano work. Gordon 
himself is in characteristically fine form on this 
worthwhile LP.

THE FIGHTIN' SIDE OF ME - Merle Haggard 
with Bonnie Owens and the Strangers - Capitol 
ST -451 
Titled after his recent hit, Merle Haggard's 
latest album is a live set recorded at a concert 
in Philadelphia. Merle, the Strangers, and Bonnie 
Owens deliver a performance "of Haggard hits 
and exciting new songs" that every Haggard fan 
is sure to want to hear. The title tune, "I Take A 
Lot Of Pride In What 
I Am" and "Okie From 
Muskogee" are among the cuts. A sure giant. 
THE KANSAS CITY SONG - Buck Owens and 
His Buckaroos - Capitol ST -476 
Teeing off with his current single smash, "The 
Kansas City Song," Buck Owens offers an album 
in which six of the songs are about or named 
after specific places (Kansas City, London, Am- 
sterdam, Texas, Scandinavia and Oklahoma). 
The rest of the numbers are about love. LP is 
certain to be a big seller. 
MY LOVE/DON'T KEEP ME HANGIN' ON - Sonny 
James and the Southern Gentlemen - Capitol 
ST -478 
The Southern Gentleman and his Southern 
Gentlemen offer a set that's bound to be a mon- 
ster. Set contains James' current single hit, 
"Don't Keep Me Hangin' On," as well as his pre- 
vious smash, "My Love," and "Ramblin' Rose," 
"Happy Memories" and a host of other tunes that 
his followers should cotton to. Stock lots of this 
THE BEST OF DEL REEVES, VOLUME II - United 
Artists UAS 6758 
Here's an album that will have both excellent 
immediate sales 
and 
substantial 
long-range 
sales. Loads of country listeners will want to pick 
up on the package, which spotlights Del Reeves 
in performances of "A Lover's Question," "Good 
Time Charlie's," "Six Days On The Road," "I've 
Used Up All My Doodle Do Do Do's" and a host 
of other numbers. "The Best Of Del 
Reeves, 
Volume II" should be showing up on the charts 
soon. 
SINGING 'EM COUNTRY - Kitty Wells - Decca 
DL 75221 
Kitty Wells' devotees will welcome the song- 
stress' latest LP effort, which showcases her in 
renderings of such tunes as "One Minute Past 
Eternity," "When The Grass Grows Over Me," 
"Tomorrow Never Comes" and "It's Written All 
Over Your Face." Also included in the package is 
a recent single of Kitty's-"I Don't See What 
I 
Saw." Set will do nicely saleswise. Keep a supply 
around. 
TOMORROW NEVER COMES - Slim Whitman - 
United Artists UAS 6763 
Slim Whitman did well on the Country Top 60 
chart with the title tune of this package, and he 
should do well with the set itself. Chanter offers 
the hit and eleven other numbers, including "My 
Heart Has A Mind Of Its Own," "Moonlight On 
The Colorado," "A World Worth Living In" and 
"Blue Canadian Rockies." LP stands an excellent 
chance of showing up on the charts.

Leslie Grade, a veteran figure in the 
British entertainment industry, has 
formed his own independent company 
Leslie Grade Ltd. just a month after 
resigning his active responsibilities 
within the EMI leisure group. The rea- 
son given for his withdrawal was 
health, and Grade has recently said 
that his new enterprise will enable him 
to function in a favorite area without 
the pressure of his EMI duties. He has 
named Albert J. Knight and Ron 
Ricardo as directors of the new com- 
pany, and Knight will again produce 
this year's Christmas pantomime at 
the London Palladium which Grade is 
presenting in association with Pye 
Records and Moss Empire chief Louis 
Benjamin. Grade is also setting up a 
major British concert tour for singing 
comedian Des O'Connor before pre- 
senting O'Connor in "The London Pal- 
ladium Revue" in Toronto next Febru- 
ary. Grade, whose brothers are Sir 
Lew Grade of Associated TeleVision 
and Bernard Delfont of the EMI orga- 
nization, has been named exclusive 
European entertainment representa- 
tive for the International and Flamingo 
Hotels in Las Vegas. His company 
will also be active in film work, with 
projects already lined up which will 
star Mireille Mathieu and Cliff Rich- 
ard. Richard will also be the main at- 
traction of the new show which Grade 
will tour around the provinces. 
Competition for available American 
disk catalogues is warming up as Bri- 
tish majors seek replacement reper- 
toire for American labels that have 
started independent operations here. 
EMI has captured the Holland-Dozier- 
Holland-Invictus and Hot Wax labels 
under a long-term deal, with Ian Mc- 
Lintock being named Invictus label 
manager in addition to his Capitol du- 
ties and Richard Smith taking charge 
of Hot Wax. As already reported Phi- 
lips has signed a pact negotiated by 
managing director Fred Marks with 
Sun vice president Noble Bell to re- 
lease Sun repertoire over the next 
three years. 
Joan Baez, The Who, Chicago, Leo- 
nard Cohen, The Doors, Mungo Jerry, 
Jimi Hendrix, Arrival, John Sehastian, 
James Taylor, Richie Havens and Pen- 
tangle are among the star names con- 
firmed to appear at the third Isle of 
Wight Music Festival on August 26th 
through 30th. Aminimum quarter mil- 
lion people are expected at the open- 
air event, whose bill last year was top- 
ped by Bob Dylan, and rumors of legal 
moves by residents in the area to ban 
the fest have not yet been confirmed. 
The shows are organized by Fiery Cre- 
ations, headed by Ron and Ray Roulk, 
who have named Tony Barrow to han- 
dle press representation for the event 
in conjunction with Fiery Creations 
publicity director Peter Harrigan. It 
will be Joan Baez's first British visit 
for three years and her only appear- 
ance here. 
Monument Records president Fred 
L. Foster and vp Bobby Weiss were in 
London for parlays with Monument 
disk licensee Decca and KPM Music, 
the affiliate of the company's Combine 
Music, where they spoke with KPM 
overseas division manager Peter Phil- 
lips and Combine's UK professional 
manager Johnny Gordon. Foster and 
Weiss were also seeking product for 
release on Monument in the States and 
other overseas markets. 
MCA Records will release in Sept- 
ember a double album entitled "Jesus 
Christ Super Star" with music written 
by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim 
Rice. Those taking part are Ian Gillan 
of Deep Purple as Christ, Yvonne Elli- 
man as Mary Magdalene, Murray 
Head as Judas Iscariot, Mike d'Abo as 
Herod, and Barry Dennen as Pontius 
Pilate. Groups involved in the project 
are Juicy Lucy, Quartermass, Nucleus, 
and the Grease Band plus a symphony 
orchestra, The City of London Ensem- 
ble, pianist John Lill and a Moog Syn- 
thesizer programmed by Mike Vickers, 
Madeline Bell, P.P. Arnold and Lesley 
Duncan are in the chorus for the work, 
which presents the last six days of 
Christ's life as observed by Judas 
Iscariot. 
Management Agency and Music has 
consolidated its recent entry into the 
music publishing field by concluding a 
deal to handle the compositions of 
Leonard Cohen in the U.K. and the 
British Commonwealth with the exclu- 
sion of Canada. The three-year pact 
was completed after three months of 
dickering between Cohen's personal 
representative 
Marty 
Mac hat 
and 
Cyril Simons, manager of Leeds Music 
which is administering the MAM pub-

Warner -Reprise celebrated its first 
birthday by purchasing 
a 
London 
Transport bus for countrywide promo- 
tional purposes. The double-decker ve- 
hicle bears the words "The Warner Re- 
prise Road Show" and the Warner 
logo, and will be used to take product 
to retailers throughout the country and 
to promote acts and records at festi- 
vals. The lower deck is being equipped 
as a discotheque and the top deck will 
be employed to sell disks at certain 
events. Warner -Reprise chief Ian Ral- 
fini revealed that the British operation 
had paid off the loan from its Amer- 
ican parent after just three months of 
business, and notched £11/4 million in 
sales during its first year. 
EMI's first cassette to be entirely 
produced in the UK has been released 
and it's "Let It Be" by The Beatles. 
The company has been tooling up for 
the last four years to manufacture its 
own tapes, and has been producing 
eight -track and four -track at its Hayes 
plant, but until now its cassettes have 
been made by the Philips factory at 
Walthamstow. EMI plans a total of 500 
cassettes on the market by the end of 
the year, predominantly pop and mid- 
dle of the road repertoire and some 
classics, with a monthly release pat- 
tern averaging twenty. Deputy mar- 
keting manager Barry Green disclosed 
details of the country's first sampler 
cassette, containing fourteen tracks by 
well known artists and selling at 29 
shillings and eleven pence. 10,000 cop- 
ies are being pressed initially for dis- 
tribution to stores with special promo- 
tion racks. 
Argo has released a two -LP boxed 
album entitled "The Wonder of the 
Age" - Mr. Edison's New Talking Pho- 
nograph" presenting the early history 
of the gramophone and including the 
voices of William Gladstone, Florence 
Nightingale, Enrico Caruso, 
Nellie 
Melba, George Bernard Shaw and P.T. 
Barnum. The album was compiled and 
produced by Kevin Daly. 
Evolution Records are launching a 
promotion campaign on two singles 
"Lovely To See You" by The Informa- 
tion and "You're Only Out To Hurt Me" 
by Abbe Jones. For the RCA van sales- 
man achieving highest sales a prize of 
£50 will be given; £25 second prize and 
£10 third prize. For the dealer with 
highest sales first prize is 2 weeks in 
Majorca; second prize one week and 
third prize a weekend in Paris. Cam- 
paign will run from July 1st thru Au- 
gust 31st. The Pathe Sound Library, 
one of the most comprehensive in 
Europe, is to be incorporated into KPM 
Music, an associate company within 
the EMI group of which Pathe is a 
member. The move will involve the 
transfer to Denmark Street of thou- 
sands of quarter inch master tapes 
containing an enormous variety of 
sounds from the splash of a drop of 
summer rain to the roar of a full scale 
battle.

ing Jazz Non -Stop series in fall

Gershwin Theme
Of 3-Day Fest
MIAMI,
FLA.—Frederick
Fennell
will
be
musical
director
and
coordi-
nator
of
the
first
festival
dedicated
exclusively
to
all
the
serious
works
of
George
Gershwin.
The
three-day
festival will be sponsored by the Uni-
versity
of
Miami
School
of
Music
October 27-28-29, 1970.
The Festival will commemorate the
50th
anniversary
of
Gershwin’s
ap-
pointment to the American Society of
Composers,
Authors
and
Publishers
(ASCAP).
An
exhibit
of
Gershwin
memorabilia —
letters,
photographs
and music—will be on display.
Fennell,
who
has
conducted
the
University
of Miami
Symphony
Or-
chestra and Symphonic Wind Ensem-
ble since 1965, will lead the Orchestra
for
the
festival,
expected
to
attract
composers, conductors and music and
film industry
personalities.
Fennell was at the Eastman School
of Music of the University of Roches-
ter from
1939
to
1962.
In
1952
he
founded
the
famous
Eastman
Wind
Ensemble,
which
has won
high
ac-
claim. From 1962 to 1964 he was as-
sociate music director of the Minneap-
olis
Symphony
Orchestra.
Columbia
University presented Fennell
its
Dit-
son
Conductor’s Award
for
1969
in
recognition
of
“his
services
to
the
A.merican
composer
in
general
and
his unique contribution to the creation
of a repertory of American works for
the wind
ensemble.”
The Festival program
for
October
27 at Dade County Auditorium in Mi-
ami
will
be Cuban
Overture,
Second
Rhapsody,
An
American
in
Paris,
Promenade,
and
Concerto
in
F.
On October 28 at the same location
the
program
will
be
Five
Preludes
for
Piano,
Lullaby,
In
a
Mandarin’s
Orchid
Garden
and A
Short
Story,
following remarks by David Ewen, a
Gershwin
biographer and
a member
of
the UM
music
faculty.
Ewen’s
book,
“George
Gershwin:
His
Jour-
ney
to
Greatness,”
is
scheduled
for
Oct.
1
publication
by
Prentice-Hall.
This
is
a
completely
re-written,
ex-
panded
and
updated
edition
of
his
1956
definitive
bio.
The third night of the festival
will
be held
at Miami Beach Auditorium.
The program
will
consist
of
“I
Got
Rhythm,”
Variations
for
piano
and
orchestra;
selections
from
the
one-
act opera, 135th
Street; Rhapsody in
Blue and major selections from Porgy
and
Bess.
All musical events will be free and
open
to
the
public,
but
tickets
will
be required. They can be obtained by
writing
George
Gershwin
Festival,
University
of Miami, P.O. Box
8073,
Coral
Gables,
Fla.
33124.
Soloists
from
the UM
School
of
Music
faculty
will
be Mary Hender-
son
Buckley,
soprano;
Eugene
Holmes,
baritone ;
Ivan
Davis
and
George
Roth,
pianists,
and
George
Zazofsky,
violinist. The Singing Hur-
ricanes,
Don
Muller
directing,
will
perform Gershwin’s choral works.

atighBox Great Britain
Belguim’s
entry
in
the
Knokke
Ca-
rousel TV
Festival was
a
half-hour
programme
featuring
British
com-
poser-singer Elton John. Happily, the
programme won the Festival compet-
ing
against
Czechoslovakia,
Spain,
Holland
and
France.
Manager
Ray
Williams
flew
across
to
partake
in
the
Award
celebrations.
John’s
American
plans
are
now
finalised
with a week at the Troubador in Los
Angeles
from
September
1st.
Ray
Williams and Steve Brown from Dick
James
Music
will
be
accompanying
the singer on
his America
visit.
Chappell
and
the
Famous
Music
Corporation
of
America
have
renewed
their
association
for
a
fur-
ther
five years. The two giants
oper-
ate
joint companies
in various
terri-
tories
under
the
name
of
Famous
(Chappell,
headed
in
London
by
former
Philips
Records
British
chief
Leslie
Gould.
Apart
from
travelling
extensively, Gould
liaises closely here
with
Frank
Coachworth
and
Teddy
Holmes
of Chappell, which
houses
a
Famous
Chappell
office
where
Tony
Peters
is
in charge of promotion and
exploitation,
but
Gould
himself
works out of the Paramount building
in Wardour Street. There
is a string
of
soundtracks coming
with
the
Fa-
mous
Chappell
copyright
imprint.
One
of them
is
“Borsalino”
starring
Jean-Paul
Belmondo
and
Alain
De-
lon, who
also
directed
the
movie.
It
opens
at
the
Paramount
Cinema
on
July
30th
and
is
a
gangster drama
set
in
Marseilles
in
the
1920s.
The
background
chart
was
penned
by
Claude
Bolling,
and
the
soundtrack
album
released
here
on
the
Paramount
label has already notched
over
200,000
sales
in
France.
Other
forthcoming
Famous
Chappell
soundtracks
are
“Darling
Dili”
star-
ring
Julie Andrews and composed by
Henry
Mancini
and
Johnny
Mercer;
“Little
Fauss And
Big
Halsy”
with
Robert Redford and music by Johnny
Cash;
“Norwood”
featuring
Glen
Campbell,
who
also
penned
eight
songs for the pic and “Peau D'Anne”
with a chart by Michel Legrand. The
latter movie reflects Paramount’s po-
licy
of
commissioning
scores
from
top writers in the countries where the
company’s
filming
activities
are
tak-
ing
place.
The
Famous
label
will
make
its
bow
here
in
September,
joining
the
Paramount
and
Dot
la-
bels
beneath
the EMI
pressing
and
distribution
banner.
Rod
Duncombe
will add
it to his Paramount and Dot
label management
duties,
and
Gould
stressed
that Famous
will
be
in
the
market for new British and continen-
tal
talent
rather
than
chasing
acts
hitherto
on
other
labels.
Bernard
Chevry’s Midem
organisa-
tion
is
adding
the
video
cassette
to
its
tally
of
yearly
occasions
at
the
Palais
des
Festivals
in
Cannes
in
1971. A Vidca meet will be held con-
currently
with
the
annual
Mip TV
convention from
April
17th
through
23rd,
and
will
consist
of
seminars
centered
on
the
new
medium
with
regard to copyright, promotion, stan-
dardisation,
and
its
specific
role
in
the
fields
of
industry
and
education
in the future as well as
in entertain-
ment.
Hardware
(equipment)
and
software
(programming)
will be
ful-
ly
covered, and Vidca
(short
for
vi-
deo cassette)
will culminate on
April
23rd with
a
final seminar summaris-
ing
the
discussions
and
decisions
of
the
previous
days.
Midem’s
British
rep Roger Watkins has been assigned
the
task
of
organising
Vidca
on
an
international
scale. Midem
itself
will
take
place on January
17th
through
22nd, but
it has been decided to make
Classical Midem a bi-annual event on
account
of
the
need
for
extensive
long-range
preparation. The
decision
was
taken
in
conjunction
with
the
International
Music
iCouncil,
which
organises
the
event
in
conjunction
with
Midem,
and
the
next
classical
meet is slated for 1972.
The
Robert Stigwood
Organisation
is
now
expected
to
make
its
stock
market
bow
some
time
in
August.
The
company
originally
planned
to
get
into
the City act
last year by
a
reverse takeover of Arbiter and Wes-
ton,
but
this
plan was
not
fulfilled.
Stigwood’s
colleague
in

'Professionalism Is Our Format' 
The most recent Pulse survey in 
the Toledo area shows WTOD a 5,000 
kw country station at the top of the 
ladder among listeners in the 18-49 
age bracket. But the picture was not 
always as rosey for WTOD; in fact, 
for years they had remained on the 
bottom rungs. Then, in September, 
1968, they decided to convert from a 
top forty to a modern country format, 
a good decision in the light of their 
phenomenal upsurge since then. 
WTOD's accomplishment is note- 
worthy since it has faced consider- 
able competition in the Toledo mar- 
ket, including three Top Forty sta- 
tions. In accounting for a country 
format station winning out in the 
ratings race, WTOD's program direc- 
tor Jim Wight commented, "At the 
same time country grew. more sophis- 
WTOD 
Toledo, Ohio. 5,000 kw. 
John Booth, pres.; Robert Martz, 
general 
mgr.; 
Charles Fleishman, 
commercial mgr.; Jim Wight, pro- 
gram dir. and promotion mgr.; Bill 
Manders, 
production 
mgr.; 
Chuck 
Wheeler, music dir.; Dick Lambert, 
news dir. 
Format: Modern Country. Playlist: 
85-90 singles, selected albums and 
Oldies. 
On -Air -Personalities: 
Jim 
Wood, 
6-9 a.m.; Jim Wight, 
9 to noon; 
Chuck Wheeler, noon to 3 p.m.; Bill 
Manders, 3-6 p.m.; Les Bortell, 6-9:15 
p.m. 
ticated, rock began to become less 
palatable to all but the teenage lis- 
teners." The inevitable result was 
that older members of the audience 
became more attracted to modern 
country sounds. 
Wight cited another important fac- 
tor, "We pay our jocks more than 
some stations in major markets. They 
work hard in promoting the station 
while they're on the air and while 
they're off. Professionalism is our 
format." 
Using the NAB recommended com- 
mercial load of 18 minutes, WTOD 
walks a line between rock or extreme 
sounding country music and what 
Wight termed "hard" or very tradi- 
tional country. Basic policy is to play 
two album tracks and two oldies per 
hour, using the remaining time to 
play selections from a playlist of 
85-90 singles. 
DROP RIGHT IN-That's what Cer- 
tron Records' Pozo Seco did at the 
studios of the Larry Kane Show in 
Houston. KTRK-TV personality Kane 
was on hand to welcome the pair, who 
brought along a copy of their new 
LP. 
Promotions are heard often on the 
station. A recent one, with the im- 
probable title "Send A Friend To 
Hell," rewarded winners with an all - 
expense paid weekend at the Satan's 
Holiday Fair in Hell, Michigan. A 
Country Clunker contest featured a 
run down 1957 station wagon as the 
first prize, while "Hi -Low" gave lis- 
teners the chance to zero in on an 
exact money figure in a fashion sim- 
ilar to the one used in the card game. 
Currently WTOD is involved in a 
whirlwind preparation for the Miss 
Lucas County Fair contest which is 
sponsored by them. In addition to 
selecting applicants, the deejays have 
the 
somewhat 
enviable 
task 
of 
screening them 
and choosing the 
finalists. Winner of the competition 
receives a bevy of WTOD-donated 
prizes. 
During the month of December, the 
station goes all out on a "Penny 
Pitch" campaign to raise money for a 
local crippled children's home. Jocks 
shovel walks, wash cars, allow pies 
to be thrown in their face, all for 
donations. "It's simply an emotional 
appeal for money," explained Wight. 
Last year the station was directly 
responsible for raising over $4,000 
for this charity. 
ABC newscasts are heard on the 
hour in addition to two minutes of 
local news. Editorials are aired four 
times per day and changed every oth- 
er day. 
Claim Unauthorized 
Lennon Video Tape 
NEW YORK - Screenings of an 
hour-long video tape on John and 
Yoko Lennon to sponsors and net- 
works in the U. S., England, and 
Japan by Anthony Cox, are being 
conducted without authorization or 
consent from either of the Lennons 
or ABKCO Industries which rep- 
resents the Lennons, according to 
ABKCO. 
It was also added that John Len- 
non is not preparing a score for the 
tape, as reported. 
Sperber & Scene '70 
Set For 26 More Weeks 
NEW YORK - Betty Sperber's op- 
tion as producer of the rock TVer, 
Scene '70, has been renewed for an- 
other 26 week cycle. Other options 
which were renewed at the same time 
include Mike Gargiulo, director, Ani- 
ta 
Tricarico, 
talent 
coordinator, 
Susan Gottlieb, production supervi- 
sor, and Danny Aharoni, production 
coordinator. Stephanie Gray has been 
named associate producer and Dave 
Rogers and John M. Kinsellagh re- 
main as executive producers. 
Scene '70, which is now seen in 84 
markets recently began a policy of 
having guest hosts for each of the 
shows. Kicking off the new format 
was James Brown. Subsequently Me- 
lanie, Johnny Maestro, Jerry Butler, 
Kenny Rogers and the First Edition 
and Oliver have served in the capacity 
with the 'Chamber Brothers, Sam 
Moore (formerly of Sam & Dave), 
Andy Kim, the Grass Roots, Richie 
Havens, Genva Ravan & Ten Wheel 
Drive and Ray Charles slated for fu- 
ture hosting duties.

Gold Decks To Jocks 
In `Parkway' Promotion 
LOS ANGELES - Two thousand 
gold records have been shipped to 
radio stations, program directors and 
disk jockies throughout the nation by 
United Artists Records and the Bullet 
Music Group in promotion for the 
just issued single, "Come With Me" 
by The Utopia Parkway. Disk was 
individually inscribed, 
and printed 
matter carried the legend that the 
souvenir gold platter is the forerun- 
ner of "a legitimately -earned similar 
award by the group in the very near 
future." 
Recording by the quartet is cur- 
rently the recipient of a heavy pro- 
motional push by the United Artists 
Records staff. 
Paulsen Named At WNEW-FM 
NEW YORK - Metromedia Radio 
has announced the appointment of 
Varner Paulsen as vice-president and 
general manager of WNEW-FM in 
New York. Most recently Paulsen 
was v.p. for administration for Me- 
tromedia and general manager of 
KNEW -San Francisco.

attention to key catalog, top steady selling LP's, as well as recent chart hits still going strong in sales. Information is supplied by manufacturers. This is a weekly 
revolving list presented in alphabetical order. It is advised that this card be kept until the list returns to this alphabetical section.

SUNN SET-Sunn Musical Equip- 
ment Co. has made available its new 
Solos guitar amplifier which has al- 
ready been pre -tested by performers 
such as Johnny Cash, the Tennessee 
Three and Hank Williams, Jr. De- 
signed for portability, the unit is 
self-contained and weighs 64 pounds 
in its 201/2" by 261/2" frame (it is 
11%" deep). The Solos has a power- 
ful 110 watts RMs output (260 watts 
pead) and using dual channels, the 
unit has treble boost on both and 
effects on channel two. It is readily 
utilized for lead, rhythm or steel and 
allows several speaker options. 
Celebration Planned 
As Vokes Enters 20th 
PITTSBURGH-Howard Vokes will 
be feted this month (the 29th) as he 
marks his 20th year in country music. 
Hosted by WEEP -Pittsburgh's Ron 
Coulter, the affair will be staged at 
the Griltz Hotel in Verona, Pa. 
Guesting will be Kaye Fouss. 
Vokes' first project marking the 
20th is a new single, "Six Men And 
One Woman."

The pressing and distribution of Lib- 
erty Records repertoire went back to 
EMI with effect from July 27th after 
talks to renegotiate the deal between 
Liberty and Philips had failed. There 
was a further nine months to run on 
the existing pact, but Liberty -UA 
London chief Martin Davis invoked a 
fail-safe clause in the contract to end 
the arrangement. Liberty thus re- 
turns to the EMI fold, where the UA 
label is already being handled, and 
the Liberty -UA sales force will now 
operate with both labels in the same 
rational neck of the woods. 
The 
agreement with EMI does not include 
the imported Blue Note jazz line or 
any tape or budget product. Davis 
was one of the indie chiefs most con- 
cerned by the horrendous hang-up 
that occurred at Phonodisk, the Phil- 
ips-Polydor 
distribution 
service, 
when it began its Ilford operation 
last Easter, but he has denied that 
this hiatus motivated the move of 
Liberty 
back 
to 
EMI. 
Philips - 
Phonodisk supremo Stephen Gottlieb 
confirmed that talks had started to 
renegotiate the Liberty -Philips deal 
but ended because the parties could 
not reach a mutually satisfactory 
financial arrangement. Davis fixed 
the pact with EMI in discussions with 
EMI Records managing director Phil- 
ip Brodie and sales and marketing 
chief Cliff Busby in which he was 
joined by Liberty -UA legal and ac- 
counting vp Sy Zucker. 
Recent activity at United Artists 
Music publishing companies indicates 
a surge of important releases be- 
tween now and the autumn. On the 
film music front singles and albums 
include the soundtrack of "Ned Kel- 
ly" which features a track by Mick 
Jagger, all other music composed by 
Shel Silverstein. Later in the year 
two major United Artists films are 
"The Private Life of Sherlock Hol- 
mes" with score by Miklos Rosza and 
"The Music Lovers" based on the life 
of Tchaikovsky with Andre Previn 
conducting the 
London Symphony 
Orchestra. Other future productions 
are "The Landlords" music by Al 
Kooper; "Cotton Comes to Harlem" 
score by Galt McDermot and "Good- 
bye Mr. Tibbs" music by Quincy 
Jones and Dave Grusin. Noel Rogers 
is excited about the current success 
of 
Shirley 
Bassey's 
version 
of 
"Something" and forecasts her Sep- 
tember album will reveal a new inter- 
pretation of contemporary, standard 
and original material. Of "Oh Calcut- 
ta," Rogers is of the opinion that it 
could be the most exciting musical 
review to arrive in London for many 
years. 
The days of open-air pop festivals 
seem to be numbered, judging by re- 
cent events. The upcoming event in 
the Isle of Wight is encountering 
difficulties in finalising a site which 
may culminate in a legal injunction 
to stop the fest taking place at all. 
At a recent public meeting in Fresh- 
water to discuss the event Brigadier 
C. G. Phipps, a county councillor, 
was howled down by a contingent of 
hippies as he tried to chair the meet- 
ing and ended up wrestling for the 
microphone with festival producer 
Rikki Farr of Fiery Creations. Island 
authorities have threatened an in- 
junction if agreement is not reached 
with Fiery Creations on festival ar- 
rangements. Meanwhile a storm of 
protest has arisen about the recent 
blues festival which took place at 
Shepton Mallet, Somerset, on the 
Bath and West Agricultural Society's 
showground. The National Farmers 
Union is complaining to the Home 
Secretary about damage done to the 
ground and the amount of garbage 
left behind, and also because a farm- 
er whose property is adjacent lost 
five hundred fencing posts and seven 
gates. The NFU is also considering 
action against members who lease 
their land for pop festivals, on ac- 
count of such hiring out for non- 
agricultural purposes of profit is 
unethical in view of the agricultural 
subsidies being paid to farmers by 
the state. The Hollywood festival in 
Staffordshire has left several credi- 
tors with egg on their faces and a 
Conservative Member of Parliament 
is seeking legal measures to stop the 
forthcoming Plumpton festival from 
taking place on behalf of objecting 
local residents. A free concert was 
staged in Hyde Park July 18th by 
Blackhill Entertainments and attend- 
ed by an estimated 50,000. It was 
marred by several ugly incidents, 
mostly caused by Hell's Angels, the 
self appointed stewards, and a hot 
dog stand overturned, giving first de- 
gree burns to a girl who was taken 
to the nearby St. George's Hospital 
in company with ten other young- 
sters on bad trips. It seems debatable 
whether the Greater London Council 
will continue to grant permission for 
these mass pop happenings in Hyde 
Park in view of these incidents and 
the underlying current of violence at 
this last concert, plus the growing 
hostility throughout the areas select- 
ed as venues for such events. 
John Morton was elected general 
secretary of the Musicians Union in 
succession to Hardie Ratcliffe, who 
retires next 
spring. Morton 
will 
resign his post as senior lecturer in 
industrial relations and administra- 
tion at Solihull Technical College at 
the end of the year and will have a 
major task on his hands when com- 
mercial radio is officially introduced 
here. He has already stipulated that 
commercial stations must use a fair 
share of live music in addition to 
records in their programming, and a 
lot of hard bargaining obviously lies 
ahead on needle time allocation. A 
July 1st increase of 33% in recording 
fees for musicians in the dance band 
and light orchestra categories means 
that the session rate has risen by £3 
to £12. 
EMI 
group 
managing 
director 
John Read denied Israeli allegations 
that the company had bowed to pres- 
sure from Arab countries in ending 
its disk pressing arrangement in Is- 
rael with the Palestine Orient compa- 
ny. The move resulted in a ban being 
imposed by Israeli Commerce Indus- 
try officials on the import of all EMI 
records. Read explained the termina- 
tion of the deal with Palestine Orient 
was in purely commercial grounds 
because EMI was not satisfied with 
merchandising arrangements.

LONDON - Stig 
Anderson 
of 
Sweden Music AB is celebrating his 
10th anniversary in the Scandinavian 
publishing and record field. He began 
his publishing activities in 1960 after 
having a hit as a songwriter with 
"Klas-Goran," and also opened up 
the Scandinavian outlet on Bens Mu- 
sic in Brussels, as well as acquiring 
American and European catalogs. In 
1965, he began his own record label 
Polar Music AB in partnership with 
Bengt 
Bernhag 
which 
established 
many local artistes, and also has 
publishing and record interests in 
Denmark and Norway. In 1969, And- 
erso 1 was awarded a Swedish "Gram-

Famous Music Catalog Thrust: 
Putting 'Diamonds In New Settings 
NEW YORK - The Famous Music 
Publishing division of Famous Music 
Corp., has just completed a catalog - 
oriented first national planning con- 
ference at its New York headquar- 
ters. The meeting was called by Fa- 
mous Music Publishing vice president 
and chief operating officer Marvin 
Cane. In attendance were the Famous 
professional staff from throughout 
the United States as well as the com- 
pany's numerous staff writers and 
Famous Music Corp. president Bill 
Gallagher. 
The meeting served a two -fold pur- 
pose in that the publishing executives 
and staff had an opportunity for mu- 
tual in depth discussions of the con- 
temporary expansion plans of the 
company as well as the chance to 
launch a new program which is de- 
signed to build upon the company's 
tradition as 
a publisher of great 
standards. 
Famous Music over the years has 
published many of the hits in musical 
history, and these songs comprise a 
catalog which has long enabled Fa- 
mous to stay among the leaders in 
the publishing industry. 'It was deter- 
mined at this conference that the val- 
ue of these songs has not been ex- 
hausted by their use in the repertoire 
of artists over the years and that 
they are in fact the base upon which 
Famous is now building its contem- 
porary catalog. 
Diamonds In New Setting 
Cane and Gallagher, in addressing 
the meeting, pointed out the current 
value of the standards catalog with 
the observation that within the last 
two years a list of some nearly 
threescore songs from it have en- 
joyed a contemporary renaissance. 
Among the 
examples 
wer 
Mama 
Cass' "Dream A Little Dream Of Me" 
and Tiny Tim's "Tip Toe Through 
The Tulips". 
Gallagher 
credited these current 
successes with older tunes to the fact 
that the songs were placed in con- 
temporary setting by the artists who 
made use of them. "A song that has 
appealed to the public is like a dia- 
mond" Gallagher stated. "Occasional- 
ly it may need a new setting but it 
always maintains its lustre." 
Incentive Program 
In line with this Cane announced 
first for the publishing industry in 
the form of an incentive program 
designed around the Famous stand- 
ards catalog. Under the program a 
man will be rewarded for activity 
Don Pierce Exits 
Starday-King 
NASHVILLE - Don Pierce, who 
founded Starday Records with Pappy 
Daily in 1952, is leaving Starday- 
King. Pierce developed a highly suc- 
cessful C&W operation moving from 
Los Angeles to Nashville in 1957. 
Pierce reports no plans at present 
except to take an extended vacation 
and continue to help the Starday- 
King operation with his knowledge 
of country music packaging, publish- 
ing, and licensing. 
Starday acquired King Records in 
1968 after the death of Don's friend 
Syd Nathan. Both Starday and King 
were sold to LIN Broadcasting in 
1968 and Hal G. Neely, a former vice 
president of King, who had become 
vice president and general manager 
of Starday, assumed the presidency 
of the combined Starday-King oper- 
ation which includes eight active la- 
bels and over twenty publishing cat- 
alogs. 
Prior to forming Starday, Pierce 
had been a motivating force in the 
4 -Star Music and Record catalogs, on 
the west coast, that was later sold to 
Gene Autry and Joe Johnson. 
Pierce is a founding director for 
the Country Music Association, a 
founding director in the Nashville 
Chapter of NARAS and is now a vice 
president of the 'Citizens Bank of 
Hendersonville, Tennessee. 
generated with these songs. The in- 
crease 
in 
exploitation 
will 
come 
about, 
in the estimation of Cane, 
through the coordination between the 
professional and writing staffs of Fa- 
mous in resetting these tunes in the 
style necessary for today's artists. 
"It is not in giving rates and selling 
short the value of a standard that 
activity is generated," noted Cane. 
"The test for a standard lies in its 
presentation in the light of today's 
market." 
The activity of Famous in all other 
areas of the 
contemporary music 
business was the other major topic of 
the conference. Famous will be en- 
gaged across the full spectrum of the 
business Cane pointed out, in the 
freedom that it enjoys not only in 
developing new writers and material 
but in producing masters in line with 
this 
development and 
in 
offering 
those masters to labels throughout 
the industry. 
Gallagher strongly made the point 
to the assembled executives and writ- 
ers that they are not tied to any 
other division of the corporation, es- 
pecially the firm's record labels. They 
must therefore make the best deal for 
product which they generate. He 
noted that Marvin Cane has long 
been associated with some of the 
finest 
publisher -initiated 
recording 
deals in the industry. "We must set 
our sights and cast off traditional 
encumberances to assure a continu- 
ance in that tradition" noted Galla- 
gher. 
In closing the conference Gallagher 
made the final point that "the music 
publishing business has, in my esti- 
mation, sat wistfully by and wit- 
nessed a new music era develop and 
has lamented the fact that they were 
not part of it. The direction at Fa- 
mous, 
however, 
is marketing 
ori- 
ented. As we continue to develop our 
contemporary writers and catalog we 
will 
also 
continually re-emphasize 
our great standards, repackaged to 
meet today's need and tastes." 
Kinney's 9 Mos. 
Sets A Record 
NEW YORK - Record earnings are 
reported by Kinney National Service, 
Inc. for the nine -month period ended 
June 30, 1970. The company owns 
Warner Bros. Pictures and the Atlan-
